The clinical presentation—chronic vulvar pruritus, dyspareunia, progressive architectural changes (labial atrophy, clitoral retraction), and characteristic white, thin, sclerotic plaques—is highly suggestive of **lichen sclerosus (LS)**. The biopsy findings—epidermal thinning, loss of rete ridges, hyperkeratosis, and dermal sclerosis—are the classic histopathologic hallmarks of LS. These features, combined with the perianal involvement (pale, wrinkled skin), further support the diagnosis. No features of malignancy (e.g., atypia, dysplasia, invasion) or other inflammatory dermatoses (e.g., lichen planus, psoriasis) are described.

**Clinical Diagnosis:** Lichen Sclerosus (Vulvar and Perianal)

- Chronic (12-month) severe vulvar pruritus  
- Progressive dyspareunia leading to sexual abstinence

- Hyperkeratosis

- Baseline and annual vulvar/perianal examination for early detection of malignant transformation
